title: From 7-Eleven to James Beard: The Improbable Rise of Chef Suresh Sundas
excerpt: The Nepali-born chef who taught himself to cook in his mother's kitchen has become the first person from Nepal to be named a James Beard Award finalist — and he's rewriting the rules of Indian food in Washington, DC.
body:
There is a moment in Suresh Sundas's story that sounds like it belongs in a film. He is 24 years old, newly arrived in the United States, working the counter at a 7-Eleven in Northern Virginia. One evening, he makes chicken curry for his roommates. A guest tries it. "This chicken curry is so good," she tells him, "you should work in a restaurant, not a 7-Eleven."

He found the nearest restaurant in Virginia the next day and got the job.

## The Kitchen as Classroom

Sundas never attended culinary school. Everything he knows about cooking he learned at home in southeastern Nepal, where he began preparing family meals at the age of eleven while his mother worked. Lentil rice, fried rice, momos — the vocabulary of a Nepali kitchen became his foundation.

His professional education came at Rasika West End, one of Washington's most acclaimed Indian restaurants, where he mastered the tandoor and absorbed the discipline of fine-dining service. It was there that he met Dante Datta, a mixologist and the son of West Bengali immigrants, whose cocktail ambitions matched Sundas's culinary ones.

## Building Daru and Tapori

In August 2021, the pair opened Daru — Hindi slang for moonshine — in the H Street corridor, a modern Indian restaurant where the cocktail programme is as inventive as the food. A Dirty Martini made with achar. Paneer pesto tikka with honey and rhubarb. Blue cheese kebabs with cashew and sour cherry. The menu is playful, boundary-crossing, and unapologetically personal.

The *New York Times* named Daru one of America's 50 best new restaurants. The Michelin Guide awarded it a Bib Gourmand. *Washingtonian* placed it in the city's top 100.

Then came Tapori, which opened in 2025, also on H Street — this one drawing on the street food traditions of the Indian subcontinent. *Eater* named it one of the 15 best new restaurants in America, a recognition that cemented Sundas and Datta as one of the most exciting partnerships in American dining.

## Making History

When the James Beard Foundation announced its 2026 finalists in March, Sundas was named in the category of Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic — the first Nepalese chef ever to receive the honour. He was also the only non-Pennsylvania chef in the running for the regional award.

At the 43rd annual RAMMY Awards — Washington's premier restaurant honours — Sundas won Rising Culinary Star of the Year, a recognition of both his talent and his trajectory.

"We wanted Daru to feel like a space where anyone could drop in, whether it's for a casual meeting, a cocktail, or to mark a celebration," Sundas has said. That democratic spirit — the same instinct that makes Indian street food so universally appealing — runs through everything he builds.

## The Diaspora Dimension

Sundas's story resonates far beyond the Nepali community. It is a story about the broader South Asian immigrant experience in America's restaurant industry — the unheralded cooks who arrive without credentials but with deep culinary knowledge absorbed from their mothers' kitchens, who work their way from convenience stores and dishpits to the highest honours in American gastronomy.

The partnership with Datta adds another layer. Here are two men — one Nepali, one Indian-American — whose collaboration reflects the fluid, boundary-crossing reality of South Asian identity in the diaspora. Their food does not fit neatly into any single regional box, and that is precisely the point.

As Tapori put it on Instagram after the James Beard nomination: "What he carries from his mother's kitchen, what he has built here, what he is building for the next generation of cooks who come from somewhere people didn't expect them to come from — that is the work. The nomination is just proof that other people see it too."

## What's Next

Both restaurants continue to evolve. Soft-shell crab season has brought local Chesapeake ingredients onto Sundas's menus, reflecting his belief that great Indian cooking in America should engage with American terroir, not just replicate what exists in India.

For the thousands of South Asian immigrants working in American kitchens right now — many of them self-taught, many of them invisible — Sundas's rise is not just inspiring. It is proof that the path exists, even when no one has walked it before.
